column2: A long narrative poem about a hero whose great deeds decide the fate of a whole people.
A great wooden hall where a lord feasted his warriors, gave them treasure, and sheltered them, making it the center of a tribe's life.
A kenning for a king, who earns his warriors' loyalty by handing out rings and treasure.
A warrior who serves a lord in exchange for the lord's protection and gifts.
The bond between a chief and his war-band, in which he gives protection and treasure and they give loyalty to the death.
An Old English court poet who composed and sang stories of heroes to the harp in the mead-hall.
A compound metaphor that names a thing by describing it, like "whale-road" for the sea.
A kenning for a person's store of words, so "unlocked his word-hoard" means he began to speak.
A kenning for a mail shirt, the woven net of iron rings that covers the chest.
The repetition of the same first sound in nearby stressed words, which binds each line of Old English poetry together in place of rhyme.
A pause in the middle of an Old English line that splits it into two half-lines linked by alliteration.
A formal public vow in which a warrior names the deed he will do and stakes his honor on doing it.
A ritual contest of insults and counter-boasts between two warriors.
A death price paid to a victim's family that settles a killing and replaces blood revenge.
The Old English idea of fate, a fixed destiny that decides how each person's life will end.
The warrior ethic that demands courage, loyalty to one's lord, revenge for slain kin, and deeds that win lasting fame.
A heavy twisted metal ring worn around the neck as a sign of wealth and rank.
Ironic understatement that stresses a point by denying its opposite, like "it was hardly a shame to be showered with such gifts."
A story inside the main story that comments on the main action through comparison or contrast.
An epic that grows out of oral tradition and has no certain author, also called a primary epic.
An epic written by a single known author, also called a literary epic.
The features that mark an epic, namely a significant hero, superhuman deeds, supernatural helpers or enemies, a vast setting, and a grand, objective style.
The standard devices of an epic, namely a theme stated at the start, a call to the Muse, opening in medias res, catalogs, formal speeches, and digressions.
Latin for "in the middle of things," meaning that a story opens in the middle of the action.
A call at the start of an epic asking a goddess of inspiration to help the poet tell the story.
A long formal list of people, ships, weapons, or gifts.
Stock phrases and epithets that oral poets reused to fill out lines and remember long poems.
Words that are recorded only once in the whole surviving written record of a language.
A meditative poem or passage that mourns the dead.
A formulaic expression of grief.
Latin for "where are they?", the name for a passage that mourns vanished people and the passing of glory.
A direct statement by the narrator of what will happen later in the story.
A feud in which the relatives of a person who was killed take revenge on the killer or his family.
An Old English elegy in which a lordless warrior mourns the loss of his lord and companions.
